title: Thesis statements, outlines, revising and editing
blurb: Spot a strong thesis, build a formal outline, and sort any change into revising or editing.
question: A student's draft opens with 'In this essay, I will talk about hospital food.' Her instructor says the thesis needs work, and later marks one paragraph that wanders off topic and three comma errors. What makes a thesis effective, and which fixes are revising versus editing?

teach.h: The thesis: one sentence, one claim
teach.body: Formally, a thesis statement is one sentence that states the main claim, or controlling idea, of an essay. A good thesis is specific, focused and, for an argument, arguable, and it often previews the main points. In plain English: it is the promise the essay keeps. Every body paragraph should help prove it. A thesis is not a plain fact, not a question, not an announcement ('In this essay I will...') and not too broad.

head: Draft thesis
Problem
rows: In this essay I will discuss clinic hours.
Our clinic should add Saturday hours for working parents.

teach.h: Narrowing a topic to a thesis

items.label: Thesis: hospitals should offer nap rooms

teach.caption: Narrowing the topic happens in prewriting, before the working thesis is drafted.

teach.body: An outline is a prewriting tool that arranges ideas in a logical order. A formal outline uses a fixed sequence of labels from broadest to most specific: Roman numerals (I.) for main points, capital letters (A.) for supporting points, Arabic numerals (1.) for details, and lowercase letters (a.) for finer details. Each level supports the one above it, so a subpoint must fit under its heading.

teach.h: A formal outline as a tree

root.label: Thesis
root.sub: Our clinic should add Saturday hours

teach.caption: I. main point, A. support, 1. detail, a. finer detail. Every branch must support the branch above.

teach.body: Revising improves content and organization: is the thesis clear, is the order logical, is there enough support, does every sentence belong, do the transitions work, and does the word choice suit the audience? Peer feedback is often used here. A handy summary is ARRR: add what is missing, rearrange what is out of order, remove what does not belong, replace what is weak.

teach.caption: Editing also covers usage, sentence structure and consistency (for example, verb tense). Proofreading is the final typo check.

teach.body: Marcus Reed's draft begins: 'In this essay I will discuss hand washing.' He rewrites it as a claim: 'Our dorm should install hand-sanitizer stations at every entrance.' Then he revises: he adds a survey result, moves his strongest reason to the end, and removes a story about his uncle that does not support the thesis. Last, he edits: he fixes two comma splices, a misspelled 'definately' and a shift from past to present tense.

teach.text: Three classic slips. (1) A thesis written as a question or a plain fact: neither makes a claim. (2) Calling comma and spelling fixes 'revising': they are editing. (3) Treating outlining as something done after the draft: outlining is prewriting.

items: Thesis: one sentence, specific, focused, arguable; not a fact, question, announcement or broad statement.
Formal outline labels run I., A., 1., a. from broadest to most specific.
Revising = content and organization (ARRR: add, rearrange, remove, replace).
Editing = grammar, usage, sentence structure, punctuation, spelling, consistency.

summary: You can now judge whether a sentence works as a thesis and fix one that is a fact, a question, an announcement or too broad. You can also read and build a formal outline and sort any change into revising or editing.

A.q: Which sentence would work best as the thesis statement of an argumentative essay?
options: In this essay, I will discuss hospital parking fees.
Do hospital parking fees burden patients' families?
Hospitals should stop charging families to park.
Many hospitals charge visitors a daily parking fee.
A.why: A thesis states a specific, arguable claim. 'Hospitals should stop charging families to park' takes a position that the essay can support with reasons.

whyNot.0: This is an announcement: it names the topic but makes no claim.
whyNot.1: A question asks; it does not state the writer's position.
whyNot.3: This is a plain fact, so there is nothing to argue or prove.

A.q: In a formal outline, which label marks the level directly below a Roman numeral heading?
options: A capital letter (A.)
An Arabic numeral (1.)
A lowercase letter (a.)
A small roman numeral (ii.)
A.why: Formal outline labels run I., A., 1., a. A capital letter marks the first level of support under a Roman numeral main point.

whyNot.1: Arabic numerals (1.) mark details under a capital-letter point, one level lower.
whyNot.2: Lowercase letters (a.) are the fourth level, below Arabic numerals.
whyNot.3: The standard sequence I., A., 1., a. does not place small roman numerals under a main heading.

A.q: Which change is an example of editing rather than revising?
options: Replacing a weak example with a stronger one
Correcting 'their' to 'there' in a sentence
Adding a paragraph that answers an objection
Rearranging the body paragraphs by importance
A.why: Fixing a wrong word form such as 'their' for 'there' corrects the language at the word level, which is editing.

whyNot.0: Replacing a weak example changes content: that is the 'replace' move in revising.
whyNot.2: Adding a paragraph adds content, which is revising.
whyNot.3: Rearranging paragraphs changes organization, which is revising.

B.q: A student's working thesis reads: 'Health care is important to everyone.' What is its main weakness?
options: It is too broad to guide a focused essay
It is phrased as a question, not a claim
It announces the topic in the first person
It is too narrow to fill a whole essay
B.why: 'Health care is important to everyone' covers a huge subject and gives no specific direction, so it is too broad to control an essay.

whyNot.1: It is a statement, not a question.
whyNot.2: It does not say 'In this essay I will...'; it makes a general statement instead.
whyNot.3: The problem is the opposite: the subject is far too large, not too small.

B.q: In the ARRR model of revising (add, rearrange, remove, replace), which move is a writer making when she changes the vague word 'things' to 'vital signs'?
options: Add
Rearrange
Remove
Replace
B.why: Swapping a vague word for a precise one replaces weak wording with stronger wording: the 'replace' move.

whyNot.0: Adding brings in new material; here one word is swapped for another.
whyNot.1: Rearranging changes the order of existing material.
whyNot.2: Removing deletes material; nothing is deleted without a substitute here.

B.q: Ana's outline includes the main heading 'II. Barriers to exercise for night-shift workers.' Which item belongs as subpoint A under that heading?
options: Benefits of a brisk morning walk
Fatigue after a twelve-hour shift
Weekend fitness classes at the hospital
History of the twelve-hour shift
B.why: A subpoint must support its heading. Fatigue after a long shift is a barrier to exercise, so it fits under heading II.

whyNot.0: A benefit of walking is not a barrier, so it belongs under a different heading.
whyNot.2: Fitness classes are a solution or resource, not a barrier.
whyNot.3: The history of shift length is background that does not name a barrier to exercise.

C.q: A draft thesis reads: 'This paper will talk about why some students drop out of nursing programs.' Which revision turns it into the most effective thesis?
options: Why do so many students drop out of their nursing programs?
Many students leave their nursing programs before graduation.
Tutoring and mentoring would cut nursing program dropouts.
This paper will explain why nursing students drop out.
C.why: This version makes a specific, arguable claim and previews the two main points (tutoring and mentoring).

whyNot.0: Turning the topic into a question still makes no claim.
whyNot.1: This is a statement of fact, so there is nothing for the essay to argue.
whyNot.3: This is still an announcement of the topic, just reworded.

C.q: In one sitting, Rosa (1) adds a transition between paragraphs two and three, (2) corrects 'it's' to 'its,' (3) deletes a sentence that does not support her thesis, and (4) fixes a run-on sentence. Which of her changes are revising?
options: 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4
1 and 2
1 and 3
C.why: Improving transitions (1) and deleting irrelevant material (3) change content and organization, which is revising. Changes 2 and 4 fix correctness, which is editing.

whyNot.0: These are both editing: a possessive pronoun fix and a sentence-structure fix.
whyNot.1: A run-on (4) is a sentence-structure error, which is fixed in editing.
whyNot.2: Correcting 'it's' to 'its' (2) is an editing fix, not revising.

C.q: Which thesis statement is the most specific and focused?
options: Exercise is good for people in many different ways.
Daily walks can lower stress for night-shift nurses.
There are many reasons why people should exercise more.
Exercise has been studied by scientists for many years.
C.why: This thesis names a specific activity (daily walks), a specific group (night-shift nurses) and a specific claim (lower stress).

whyNot.0: 'Good for people in many different ways' is too broad and vague to guide an essay.
whyNot.2: 'Many reasons' and 'people' are vague: no specific claim or group is named.
whyNot.3: This is a general statement of fact, not an arguable claim.

reteach.title: An essay is a road trip
reteach.question: Imagine planning a road trip. What part of the trip matches the thesis, the outline, revising and editing?

blocks.body: The thesis is the destination typed into the GPS. 'Somewhere in Texas' is too broad; 'Is Texas nice?' is a question, not an address. The outline is the route: highways (I.), exits (A.), turns (1.). Revising is rerouting: adding a stop, skipping a road that leads nowhere, changing the order. Editing is the tune-up: checking the tires and signals so the car runs correctly, without changing where you are going.

blocks.text: A tune-up never changes the destination, and editing never changes the ideas. If the change alters what the essay says or where it goes, it is revising.

explain.body: A thesis is one sentence stating the essay's main claim or controlling idea. It is specific, focused and arguable, and it often previews the main points the body will develop.

test.q: What is the main purpose of a thesis statement?
options: To state the essay's controlling idea
To list every source the essay will cite
To grab attention with a surprising question
To sum up the last body paragraph's detail
test.why: The thesis states the main claim or controlling idea that the whole essay supports.

whyNot.1: Sources are listed in the reference list or works cited, not in the thesis.
whyNot.2: A question can be a hook, but a thesis makes a claim rather than asking.
whyNot.3: The thesis covers the whole essay, not one paragraph's detail.

explain.body: A weak thesis is often a plain fact (nothing to prove), a question (no claim), an announcement such as 'In this paper I will...' (no claim), or too broad (no focus).

test.q: Which draft thesis is weak because it is an announcement?
options: Flu shots should be free for all college students.
In this paper, I will be writing about flu shots.
Should college students get free flu shots?
Flu shots are given in the fall at many campuses.
test.why: 'In this paper, I will be writing about...' announces the topic without stating any claim.

whyNot.0: This is a strong thesis: a specific, arguable claim.
whyNot.2: This is weak because it is a question, not an announcement.
whyNot.3: This is weak because it is a plain fact, not an announcement.

explain.body: Built during prewriting. Labels run from broadest to most specific: I. main point, A. supporting point, 1. detail, a. finer detail. Each item must support the one above it.

test.q: In a formal outline, which sequence of labels runs from the broadest level to the most specific?
test.why: Roman numerals mark main points, capital letters mark support, Arabic numerals mark details and lowercase letters mark finer details.

whyNot.0: Capital letters sit under Roman numerals, not above them.
whyNot.1: Capital letters come before Arabic numerals in the hierarchy.
whyNot.3: This reverses the top of the hierarchy: Roman numerals are the broadest level.

explain.body: Revising changes content and organization (ARRR: add, rearrange, remove, replace). Editing fixes the language: grammar, usage, sentence structure, punctuation, spelling and consistency.

test.q: Which task is part of editing?
options: Strengthening the thesis claim
Adding evidence to paragraph two
Removing an off-topic sentence
Making verb tenses consistent
test.why: Making verb tenses consistent fixes the correctness of the language, which is editing.

whyNot.0: Strengthening the thesis changes the content of the main claim: revising.
whyNot.2: Removing an off-topic sentence improves unity: revising.
